Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:
In the 2004 Judge Penalty Guidelines there is:

---

151. Unsportsmanlike Conduct - Minor

Definition:
Minor Unsportsmanlike Conduct is defined as behavior
that may be disruptive to a person at the tournament,
but has no significant impact on the operation of
the tournament in any way.

Example:
(A) A player uses inappropriate language.
(B) A player loudly demands to a judge that her
opponent receive a penalty.

Philosophy:
Different levels of Unsportsmanlike conduct should be
penalized accordingly. The head judge is always the
final authority on what constitutes Unsportsmanlike
conduct and is free to interpret the guidelines as
he or she sees fit for the appropriate situation.

Penalty:
Warning.

---

Question: What, in practice, constitutes "inappropriate
language"?

I'm asking because I seem to have a problem with
grasping the thin line the designers thought was
apporopriate between the game and reality. Therefor
what I think is inappropriate (e.g. harsh cussing,
offensive personal remarks, etc.) could just be a
legitimate part of acting on a role.

In fact, it makes me wonder whether "inappropriate"
in the sense of "inappropriate to an age-old
methuselah" (the role we are supposedly playing in
this card game) is not basically using non-archaic
vocabulary or pronounciation.

Or is the distinction between during-the-game
tabletalk (where everything is allowed) and
between-the-games smalltalk (where the players are
out of their roles, and therefor are subject to the
rules of having to restrain themselves in terms of
getting personal)?

The point seems to be being disruptive to the person
- but I'm not sure what to determine that upon. Is
the decisive element whether the offended player is
personally disrupted by something? Or is it whether
the judge would be, in the player's place, offended
by the offense? Or is it in accordance with some
specific social/moral codes?

--
Bye,

Daneel

The general definition talking about behavior that "may be disruptive
to a person at the tournament" is not the same as "being disruptive to
a person". The judge doesn't have to prove or even find evidence that
it disrupted a person at the event. The judge only needs to decide
whether or not the behavior in general may be disruptive in nature.
For instance, I was once warned for language even though the judge
hadn't polled all of the players and audience to find out if any one of
them found my language disruptive.

-Robert

Hello Daneel,

>>> Question: What, in practice, constitutes "inappropriate
>>> language"?
>>
>> Whatever is not appropriate.
>

> What guidelines should a judge use when determining
> whether something is appropriate?

Though I personally think this topic is pretty straightforward, if you
have questions about it, I recommend the use of a case study. Describe
a *specific* example, and then experienced judges will share how they
would deal with the situation.

If you ask about the general case, the answer from LSJ will almost
always be "the judge uses his judgement," which is absolutely correct,
helpful in some ways, and useless in other ways.

If you ask about a *specific case* of judgement, then LSJ probably
won't answer, but you'll still get useful feedback from experienced
judges who will share their opinions.

I continue to believe that case studies are one of the most effective
ways to teach judges, and to create a consistency of judgement among
judges (which I think should be a goal.)

Ira

Shouldn't players get the same rulings from judges whereever they play?
If judges weren't bound to some standard rulings, the whole tournament
traveller thing could get shaky, since you couldn't know what to
expect. Allowing pet judges with pet rulings is tantamount to
introducing house rules to sanctioned tournaments, which is a bad
thing. If a judge wants to organize a tournament by his own rules, it
should be unsanctioned, and it should state which specific rules are
changed for that tournament. In order to do that, you need a consistent
catalog of rulings and rules, so you can state which ones aren't in
effect for that event.

> It is simple darwinism. More diversity makes for better judging.
>

But not on the tournament floor, where it just leads to confusion. If a
judge is unhappy with a ruling and can make a clear statement why he
feels that way he can always appeal to the rule team and LSJ. If he has
a point, he will be considered. The same applies to players: if a judge
consistently ignores consensus, a player should be able to complain
about that based on reference to which ruling that judge chooses to
ignore.

To give Godwin's law a nudge: If you merge legislative and jurisdictive
bodies, you will create a bad, bad environment for open tournaments.

Oliver

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Olive...@gmail.com wrote:
> Shouldn't players get the same rulings from judges whereever they play?

About societal expectations (i.e., community standards)? Only insafar
as "same ruling" means "apply current/appropriate societal expectations
as they are".

> If judges weren't bound to some standard rulings, the whole tournament
> traveller thing could get shaky, since you couldn't know what to
> expect.

The solution is to make the effort to make things clear and have things
that you perceive as possibly ambiguous made clear to you (both when
visiting and when receiving visitors), until everyone present
understands what community standards they have developed (the community
made up of the players present, that is).

> Allowing pet judges with pet rulings is tantamount to
> introducing house rules to sanctioned tournaments, which is a bad
> thing. If a judge wants to organize a tournament by his own rules, it
> should be unsanctioned, and it should state which specific rules are
> changed for that tournament. In order to do that, you need a consistent
> catalog of rulings and rules, so you can state which ones aren't in
> effect for that event.

We're not talking about house rules or pet rulings.

An exhaustive catalog of situational judgments would simply lead to
lawyerism -- it would be too unwieldy to be used in the noble sense you
imagine and would instead just be used as fodder for the players who
wish to twist this-or-that judgment (often out of context) to gain an
inappropriate advantage.

> The same applies to players: if a judge
> consistently ignores consensus, a player should be able to complain
> about that based on reference to which ruling that judge chooses to
> ignore.

That's not necessary.

If a judge consistenty performs poorly, players can and should report
that to the V:EKN (contacting either myself or Robert Goudie or Stewart
Wieck or Oscar Garza directly, as they like).
